I read through those and I don't think they answer my primary concern with this requirement which is whether it is achievable or not. I think my current wording at least provides a guideline for testing even if implementing it is challenging (due to the difficulty of knowing what is exploitable).
I read through those and I don't think they answer my primary concern with this requirement.

The word "exploitable" here is vague. If there is clear SQLi, command injection, or something like that, it is clear. But if it provides a weakness, that independently seems "not important", but chaining with other vulnerabilities it can become a critical factor for a successful attack to happen or not.

Also, I don't see a huge problem with being up-to-date. You need to have all components mapped, with the source etc. What is not achievable here?

To have components up-to-date is critical for L1. It can be more important than SQL injection in the application - because SQL injection from custom code someone needs to find separately, not up-to-date components are subject to automated mass-attack,s and the application is "pwned" without being targeted. The likelihood is usually high in this situation.

If you can find better wording for that, let's see that. I'm ok with the current solution and with L1.

Everyone here is right.  This is all about a huge trade off when it comes to library updates.

It is very debatable as to wether you should keep all libraries up to date. Especially if you are a fast early mover. You might update super fast, and get hit with a purposely malicious update where someone compromises the library. It's happened plenty.

But the less you actually keep libraries up to date, the more difficult it will be to update them when you are forced to do so.

There are quite a few other tradeoffs here that folks above have discussed.

So what is the real risk? The bottom line is, we do not want libraries live that can be attacked. Period. The rest is about process, time and other secondary factors. _**But proving exploitability in the world of third-party libraries is super expensive and time consuming, and is nearly impossible at scale in a big company with thousands of libraries and updates. There is no way in hell a big corp is going to prove exploitability for each library update, they do not have enough resources.**._

So I suggest as an imperfect middle-ground:

| # | Description | L1 | L2 | L3 | CWE |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
10.6.1 | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 14.2.1] Verify that only component versions without known vulnerabilities are in use. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓

> Verify that only component versions without known vulnerabilities are in use.

Is it also requirement for L3 with the same wording?

> Verify that only component versions without known vulnerabilities are in use.

* is it also requirement for L3 with the same wording?
* some may also argue, that there is component with known vulnerability but it is not exploitable in my environment

> But proving exploitability in the world of third-party libraries is super expensive and time consuming, and is nearly impossible at scale in a big company with thousands of libraries and updates. There is no way in hell a big corp is going to prove exploitability for each library update, they do not have enough resources.

I know. When I say "_Verify that only component versions without exploitable vulnerabilities are in use._", my intention is to put the onus on a verifier to prove that the application contains exploitable vulnerabilities. Clearly the app developer cannot verify this so the only way to prove that the app violates this requirement is for the verifier / pen tester to exploit the vulnerability.

> Verify that only component versions without known vulnerabilities are in use.

So the company fails requirement this if they use a component containing a CVE rated as low? 





I have an alternative proposal, I think maybe we need to replace this with a documentation requirement?

"_Verify that the application documentation defines a clear risk based remediation time frame for vulnerable 3rd party libraries vulnerabilities and that the application does not contain components which have breached these time frames._"

I think this would be an acceptable L1 requirement although we could think if we wanted to strengthen it for higher levels. It would not be super easy to verify but I agree that it is am important topic and the most important thing is to have a clearly documented policy which is followed. It is borderline a process vulnerability but I don't think there is any escaping that.

For me it seems that you are so much blinded and in love with the theory "the latest release may contain a security hole", that you are losing the focus what is the actual problem to solve here.

If you could do the stats - what is most likely the most secure release? The latest one or something from the past?

---

I recommend to change the focus here: the problem to solve is "how to mitigate the risk - downgrade the likelihood and the impact - from security weaknesses from the used 3rd party components".

Clearly, there is no "one fits all" solution. Being up-to-date in my opinion is a way better solution than "for all components, analyze all versions from that are newer than you use, analyze all known CVE's from those and measure, are you potentially affected" and this all relies on hope that there is no "silent fix" for a critical vulnerability. Convince me that it is somehow cheaper, easier or more secure way to handle it than being up-to-date.

Proposed direction:
> Verify that the risk of using vulnerable 3rd party component (version) is minimized by using up to date or latest "known to be safe" version, -add here your other options-

> > Can you expand on how you would verify this?
> 
> I don't get the point of subgoal for the question, because - you need to have an inventory, you need to have info about repos from where components are taken, so you have information about the version you use and the source from where you can detect the latest version.
> 
> It is too obvious answer for that question so I'm not sure it was the actual point for that question.

Your current proposal is something along the lines of:

'_Verify that the risk of using vulnerable 3rd party component (version) is minimized by using up to date or latest "known to be safe" version._'

How do you verify that? Clearly it is not possible "black box". So that takes us to whitebox. Does the tester have to run an SCA tool on their entire codebase? Does the application owner have to have an SCA tool running (which is what you would call a hidden requirement 😀)?

Without an SCA, this seems like an impossible task unless you can tell me otherwise so let's assume there is an SCA tool running.

SCA tools usually report on vulnerabilities, but that is not what you are asking, You are asking, are they running the most recent version of the library. So you now need to analyse the SCA report to try and figure out what the most recent version of each library is and whether they are using it. Now you didn't say it but do you mean most recent version or most recent supported versions? Many libraries will have a couple of supported minor or major versions so we need to clarify what we mean about that. We also need to hope that the SCA tool can provide that distinction.


My overall point here is that even verifying this requirement seems incredibly complicated and time consuming. 

Actually complying with it for any reasonably sized application would probably bankrupt the organization.


> Being up-to-date in my opinion is a way better solution than "for all components, analyze all versions from that are newer than you use, analyze all known CVE's from those and measure, are you potentially affected" and this all relies on hope that there is no "silent fix" for a critical vulnerability. Convince me that it is somehow cheaper, easier or more secure way to handle it than being up-to-date.

If you are just getting started then I would probably agree with you, although from a software engineering perspective it would be a complete change in common practice. It would also have a massive impact on the speed of development which no one wants to hear about.

Once an application is already functional and has amassed technical debt, the always being up to date option is no longer practical.
